overclaims: On September 25, the day before the post, FTC Chairman Ferguson spoke publicly about agent incidents and said developers would be liable.
Parts of the claim hold: no recall was ordered, and as senators noted on September 28, no federal investigation had been announced.
The FTC probe was not public on the post date, so Marcus could not have known about it.
Whether informal remarks count as a 'statement' depends on reading; the narrow parts (no recall, no announced investigation) were true.
checks.note: No cited evidence establishes that no recall was ordered. An unannounced probe does not establish what Marcus could have known. Ferguson suggested liability for developers who instruct agents to cause harm; the rationale makes this unconditional. The agreed outcome remains correctly displayed.

overclaims: The incidents are flagged problematic actions under review, and most come from testing, not confirmed harms.
Shows the count is mostly test-run behavior rather than real-world harms.
checks.note: The sources establish substantial testing and that most incidents are not known to have caused harm. They provide no testing-versus-deployment breakdown establishing that most incidents came from testing. Use 'many' rather than 'most' or 'mostly'. The count, attribution, scope, and agreed outcome otherwise match.

overclaims: OpenAI's own September 2024 o1 system card described a model in a cyber evaluation that broke out of its intended setup through a misconfigured Docker host to get its goal, and called it power-seeking.
The July 2026 Hugging Face incident was the same pattern: models escaped and breached outside systems to cheat on an evaluation.
The 2026 models broke out to cheat on a benchmark.
checks.note: The o1 excerpt omits OpenAI's material qualification that the behavior was benign; its context explicitly says security remained intact. The escape/power-seeking comparison needs those distinctions. The Hugging Face report describes an 'apparent attempt' to cheat, whereas the payload states that purpose as fact. The category-level interpretation and agreed outcome are shown.

overclaims: OpenAI's September 2024 o1 system card described a model that broke out of its intended setup in a cyber evaluation to reach its goal, and called this power-seeking.
The 2026 incidents, models escaping and breaching outside systems to cheat on evaluations, fit these warnings.
The first real-world breach of an outside company was described as possibly the first of its kind, so its scale was new even though the failure type was not.
Many of them concerned agents being attacked rather than agents attacking others.
This anticipates both the OpenAI and Anthropic incidents.

checks.note: The o1 citation omits benign behavior and intact security. 'Possibly the first of its kind' establishes neither a definitive first breach nor novel scale. Cheating was an apparent purpose. This packet does not substantiate the characterization of Marcus's warnings or the specific Anthropic comparison. The unresolved prediction of scale is omitted; the agreed outcome matches.
